title: Monolith vs Microservices
subtitle: Watch one checkout move from a single codebase to separate services, and see what you gain and what the network costs.
learn: What a monolith and a modular monolith are, and why the second is often the better start
How to draw service boundaries around business capabilities, not technical layers
Why each service must own its data, and what you give up (joins, easy transactions)
The costs of distribution: latency, partial failure, availability that multiplies, harder debugging
When splitting is worth it and when it is premature

steps.title: One app does everything
steps.body: A small shop runs as a single deployable program, a monolith. Checkout touches orders, payments, and inventory, but they all live in one process and share one database. Calling another part of the code is an ordinary function call. As the team grows from 5 to 50 people, should this one program be broken up, and what would that cost?
steps.idea: A monolith is one deployable unit; its internal calls are cheap and its transactions are simple.
steps.caption: Checkout runs entirely inside one process.

steps.title: Modular monolith first
steps.body: Before splitting anything, split the code. A modular monolith keeps one deployment but divides it into modules such as orders, payments, and inventory. Each module exposes a small interface and keeps its own tables; other modules may not reach into them. Enforce this with build-time checks or package visibility rules, otherwise boundaries erode. Calls stay in-process, so there is no network and one transaction still works, though it still deploys and scales as one unit.
steps.idea: Clear module boundaries inside one deployable give most of the design benefit of microservices without the network cost.
steps.caption: One process, but each module owns its own tables.

steps.title: Draw boundaries by capability
steps.body: When one team or one module truly needs to ship on its own, extract it. Cut along business capabilities (orders, payments, catalog), not technical layers like 'all the controllers'. A good service boundary changes for one reason and is owned by one team. Here Orders and Payments become separate services behind an API gateway, the single front door that routes each request to the right service.
steps.idea: A good service matches a business capability and one team, so most changes touch only one service.
steps.caption: The gateway now routes to the Orders service.

steps.title: Each service owns its data
steps.body: Payments has its own database, and only the Payments service may read or write it. Everyone else must ask through its API. This lets Payments change its schema or even its database engine without breaking others. The price is that you can no longer join orders to payments in one SQL query or wrap both in one transaction. Sharing a database between services quietly rebuilds the monolith. Checkout now spans three boxes, so latency and availability worsen; the next step explains by how much.
steps.idea: Owning data is what makes services independent; a shared database ties them back together.
steps.caption: Orders asks Payments by API; reaching into its DB is forbidden.

steps.title: A function call became a network call
steps.body: An in-process call takes well under a microsecond. A network round trip in one data center takes about 0.5 to 2 ms with warm connections, plus serializing (turning data into bytes to send), TLS and routing, so two extra hops move checkout from about 30 to 36 ms. Count each box in the path as 99.9% available, its database included: gateway plus app gives about 99.8% (17.5 h down a year); gateway, Orders and Payments give about 99.7% (0.999 cubed, 26 h), assuming independent failures. Partial failure means some services fail while others work, and one checkout spans three logs, so pass a trace ID along every call.
steps.idea: Every network hop adds latency and a new way to fail, and chained availabilities multiply.
steps.caption: Latency and failure risk rise with each hop.

steps.title: No cross-service transaction
steps.body: The monolith placed the order and the payment in one database transaction. Now they are in two databases. Orders can publish an OrderPlaced event to a queue and let Payments handle it later. That decouples them, but data is only eventually consistent: an order exists that is not yet paid. The client gets its answer once the event is queued, so checkout looks faster, but the payment result arrives later, and accepting an order no longer fails just because Payments is down (the queue is now a dependency). Keeping the order write and the publish in step, and charging once if a message is redelivered, are covered in the Outbox and Idempotency lessons.
steps.idea: Splitting data trades one atomic transaction for eventual consistency you must design around.
steps.caption: Orders publishes an event; Payments consumes it later.

steps.title: Payments gets slow
steps.body: Suppose Payments starts taking 3 seconds per call because its provider is struggling, and Orders has no timeout set. Orders keeps waiting, each waiting request holds a thread, and soon Orders has no free threads either. A fault in one service has spread to its callers, a cascading failure. Short timeouts, limited retries, and circuit breakers are the defence; the Timeouts and Retries lesson covers them in detail.
steps.idea: In a distributed system a slow dependency is as dangerous as a dead one, because callers pile up waiting.
steps.caption: Orders is stuck waiting on a slow Payments.

steps.title: When splitting pays off
steps.body: Microservices buy independent deploys, independent scaling, and team autonomy, which matter once many teams collide in one codebase or one module needs very different scaling. They cost you distributed debugging, versioned APIs, many pipelines, and on-call for more moving parts. As a rough rule of thumb, a single team or a handful of engineers is usually faster with a well-structured modular monolith; consider splitting when several teams keep blocking each other or one part needs very different scaling.
steps.idea: Split because of a specific pain, such as team contention or scaling, not because microservices sound modern.
steps.caption: Same checkout, two shapes: one process or separate services.

steps.title: Monolith, modular, or micro
steps.body: A monolith is simple and fast inside; a modular monolith keeps that while enforcing boundaries. Microservices cut along business capabilities and each owns its data, giving independent deploys and scaling. The price is network latency, partial failures, multiplied availability, no easy cross-service transaction, and harder debugging. Start modular, and split deliberately.
steps.idea: Boundaries first, network second: make the modules clean before you make them remote.
steps.caption: Orders and Payments run separately, each with its own DB.

quiz.q: A team wants cleaner code boundaries but has 8 engineers and one product. What is usually the best first move?
options: Build a modular monolith with enforced module interfaces
Give every module direct access to every table
Move all data into one shared service database
quiz.why: A modular monolith gives clear boundaries and ownership without network calls or distributed transactions, which a small team does not need yet.

quiz.q: Orders and Payments are separate services, but both read and write the same database tables. What is the main problem?
options: They cannot be deployed at all
The database will refuse more than one client
A schema change in one can break the other, so they are not truly independent
quiz.why: Shared tables couple the services at the data level. Independent deploys and schema changes need each service to own its data and expose it only through an API.

quiz.q: A request passes through a gateway and two services in a chain, each 99.9% available with its database counted inside. Roughly what is the availability of the whole chain?
quiz.why: Availabilities in series multiply: 0.999 x 0.999 x 0.999 is about 0.997, so every extra hard dependency lowers the total.

quiz.q: Which split follows a good service boundary?
options: A Payments service owned by one team that changes for payment reasons
A controllers service, a models service, and a views service
A Catalog service per database table that every team shares
One service per developer, each owning a slice of every feature
quiz.why: Good boundaries follow business capabilities with a single owning team. Technical layers force almost every feature to change all services at once.

quiz.q: After extracting Payments, Orders calls it synchronously and Payments becomes very slow. What can happen if Orders has no timeout?
options: Orders automatically fails fast because the platform adds timeouts
Orders threads pile up waiting, and Orders starts failing too
Nothing, because slow is not a failure
quiz.why: Waiting callers hold threads and connections. Without timeouts the slowness cascades upstream and takes the caller down as well.

cheatsheet.def: One deployable unit containing all features, usually with a single database. Simple to build, test, and run; scales and deploys as a whole.
A monolith divided into modules with explicit interfaces and private data. Gives clear boundaries without network calls.
The line around a business capability owned by one team. Good boundaries change for one reason and need few cross-service calls.
Each service alone reads and writes its data; others use its API. Enables independent change but removes joins and shared transactions.
Roughly 0.5 to 2 ms inside a data center, versus nanoseconds in-process, plus serialization and new failure modes.
Multiply the availabilities of hard dependencies, assuming independent failures: gateway, Orders and Payments at 99.9% each give about 99.7%.
A slow or failing service exhausts its callers' threads, spreading the outage upstream. Fight it with timeouts and circuit breakers.
Data in separate stores agrees after a short delay rather than instantly. The usual price of splitting data across services.
